questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a laparoscopic hernia repair under general anesthesia at 0900. At 0715, the client tells the nurse, "I had a coffee with cream on the way here about an hour ago." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the anesthesia provider before the client goes to surgery
Continue the preparation, since coffee counts as a clear liquid for surgery
Give the client an antacid and proceed with the preparation
Document the intake and send the client to surgery on time

rationale.correct: Fasting guidelines are commonly about 2 hours for clear liquids, 6 hours for a light meal and longer for fatty foods; report any deviation.

perOption.a: Recent intake raises aspiration risk, and the anesthesia team decides whether to delay.
perOption.b: Coffee with cream is not a clear liquid, and the aspiration risk must be reported.
perOption.c: The nurse cannot make this decision alone.
perOption.d: Documenting alone does not address the risk.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a breach of preoperative fasting.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old client having a knee replacement tomorrow takes metoprolol, warfarin, metformin and ginkgo biloba at home. The surgeon's instructions were reviewed last week. Which medication is usually continued with a sip of water on the morning of surgery?

options.text: Metoprolol
Warfarin
Metformin
Ginkgo biloba

rationale.correct: Follow the surgeon's and anesthesia team's instructions; beta-blockers are generally continued, while anticoagulants and some diabetes drugs are held.

perOption.a: Beta-blockers are continued to prevent rebound tachycardia and perioperative ischemia.
perOption.b: Warfarin is usually stopped several days before surgery as directed.
perOption.c: Metformin is often held on the day of surgery.
perOption.d: Ginkgo increases bleeding and is stopped before surgery.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify medications usually continued before surgery.

questions.stem: During the preoperative interview for a hip replacement next week, a 68-year-old client lists several supplements taken daily for general health, memory and joint pain. Which supplement should the nurse report because it increases bleeding risk?

options.text: Ginkgo biloba
Vitamin C
Calcium carbonate
A probiotic capsule

rationale.correct: Garlic, ginkgo, ginseng and fish oil can increase bleeding; ask about every supplement.

perOption.a: Ginkgo inhibits platelet function.
perOption.b: Vitamin C does not increase bleeding.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify supplements that increase surgical bleeding.

questions.stem: A client is having a right knee arthroscopy. The site was marked and the consent checked in the preoperative area. When should the surgical team perform the time-out?

options.text: Just before the incision, with the whole team confirming
In the preoperative area, when the site is marked
After the incision, once the joint is visible on the screen
If the surgeon or nurse has a concern about the site

rationale.correct: Universal Protocol: preprocedure verification, site marking and a time-out just before the incision.

perOption.a: The time-out is the final check, right before the incision, to prevent wrong-site surgery.
perOption.b: This is site marking, a separate step.
perOption.c: This is too late to prevent an error.
perOption.d: It is required for every procedure.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for surgery on the left shoulder. In the preoperative area, the client asks who will mark the surgical site. What is the correct answer?

options.text: "The surgeon doing the operation, while you're awake and can confirm it."
"The circulating nurse will mark it once you are asleep in the operating room."
"You'll mark the site yourself with this pen before you change."
"Marking isn't needed, because the schedule says which side."

rationale.correct: The person doing the procedure marks the site, with the client's involvement when possible.

perOption.a: The person doing the procedure marks the site, with the client involved.
perOption.b: The client must be involved in marking.
perOption.c: The surgeon is responsible for marking.
perOption.d: Marking is required for procedures involving left and right.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client who smokes is scheduled for an open colon resection. Which topics should the nurse include in preoperative teaching? Select all that apply.

options.text: How to use an incentive spirometer
Leg exercises and walking soon after surgery
Holding a pillow over the incision to cough
Rating pain on a 0 to 10 scale
Trying not to cough after surgery to protect the incision
Staying in bed for 3 days so that the incision can heal

rationale.correct: Preoperative teaching: breathing exercises, mobility, splinting, pain management and what to expect.

perOption.a: This prevents atelectasis.
perOption.b: These prevent DVT.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes into general anesthesia with sevoflurane and succinylcholine, a healthy 24-year-old client having an elective knee repair has a sudden rise in end-tidal CO2, jaw rigidity, a heart rate of 140/min and a rising temperature. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Malignant hyperthermia
Early septic shock
Hypovolemia from blood loss
An allergic reaction to latex

rationale.correct: Malignant hyperthermia: stop the triggering agents, give dantrolene, cool the client and treat hyperkalemia and acidosis.

perOption.a: This is a genetic reaction to volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine; the treatment is dantrolene.
perOption.b: The onset is too rapid and tied to the anesthetic.
perOption.c: This does not explain the rigidity and rising CO2.
perOption.d: This does not fit the rigidity and rising CO2.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client arrives in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) after a hysterectomy under general anesthesia. What should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Airway and breathing
Pain score
Abdominal dressing
Urine output

rationale.correct: PACU priorities: airway, breathing, circulation, then level of consciousness, pain and the surgical site.

perOption.a: Anesthesia and opioids depress breathing, so the airway comes first.
perOption.b: This comes after the ABCs.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Moments after extubation in the PACU, a client has high-pitched crowing sounds on inspiration, strong chest retractions and an SpO2 falling from 96% to 84%. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give oxygen with a jaw thrust and positive pressure
Give IV naloxone for the opioid effect
Suction the mouth and wait for the spasm to stop on its own
Sit the client up and coach slow breathing

rationale.correct: Laryngospasm after extubation: call for help, give 100% oxygen with positive pressure and a jaw thrust, and prepare for a small dose of succinylcholine and reintubation.

perOption.a: This is laryngospasm; 100% oxygen with positive pressure and a jaw thrust often breaks the spasm.
perOption.b: This is not opioid sedation; the airway is in spasm.
perOption.d: The client cannot move air past the closed cords.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two hours after a total abdominal hysterectomy, a client's heart rate has risen from 84 to 118/min, the blood pressure has fallen from 128/78 to 92/58 mm Hg, and the client is restless. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check the dressing, perineal pad and drains for bleeding
Give the prescribed IV morphine for the restlessness
Help the client walk to the bathroom to empty the bladder
Reassess the vital signs in 1 hour as planned

rationale.correct: Watch for hemorrhage after surgery: tachycardia, hypotension, restlessness and bleeding from dressings or drains.

perOption.a: These signs suggest hemorrhage.
perOption.b: An opioid could worsen the hypotension and hide the problem.
perOption.c: Walking is not safe with these vital signs.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the first day after an open cholecystectomy, a client who smokes has a temperature of 37.9 °C (100.2 °F) and diminished breath sounds at both lung bases. The incision is clean. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Encourage incentive spirometry, deep breaths and walking
Expect the provider to treat an infection of the incision
Restrict fluids to reduce congestion in the client's lungs
Keep the client in bed to conserve energy for healing

rationale.correct: Early postoperative fever is most often from atelectasis; treat with lung expansion and mobility.

perOption.a: These findings suggest atelectasis.
perOption.b: Wound infections usually appear around day 5 to 7.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The surgical nurse is reviewing four clients who each developed a new problem at a different point after abdominal surgery. For each finding, choose the most likely cause.

rows.text: Day 1: low-grade fever with diminished breath sounds at the bases
Day 3: burning on urination after the catheter was removed
Day 6: red incision with purulent drainage
Day 5: swelling and pain in one calf

rationale.correct: Postoperative fever timeline: wind (days 1 to 2), water (days 3 to 5), wound (days 5 to 7), walking (DVT, day 5 and later) and wonder drugs.

perOption.r1:c1: Atelectasis is the usual cause of fever in the first 1 to 2 days.
perOption.r1:c2: UTIs usually appear around day 3 to 5.
perOption.r1:c3: Wound infections usually appear around day 5 to 7.
perOption.r1:c4: DVT does not cause diminished breath sounds.
perOption.r2:c2: Catheterization raises the risk of UTI.
perOption.r3:c3: Purulent drainage and redness indicate wound infection.
perOption.r4:c4: Calf swelling on one side suggests DVT.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Link postoperative complications to their timing.

questions.stem: A client is receiving IV midazolam and fentanyl for moderate sedation during a colonoscopy. Which monitoring is most important during the procedure?

options.text: Continuous SpO2, breathing and level of consciousness
Capillary blood glucose every hour of the procedure
Temperature every 15 minutes until the procedure ends
Urine output every 15 minutes through a catheter

rationale.correct: Procedural sedation: continuous pulse oximetry and capnography, vital signs, sedation level, and reversal agents at hand.

perOption.a: Sedatives and opioids together can depress breathing.
perOption.b: This is not the main risk.
perOption.c: This is not the main risk.
perOption.d: This is not the main risk.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Monitor a client during moderate sedation.

questions.stem: During moderate sedation with midazolam alone, a client becomes unresponsive to voice with slow, shallow breathing. The nurse has opened the airway and is giving oxygen, and the SpO2 is now 88%. Which reversal agent should the nurse have ready?

options.text: Flumazenil
Naloxone
Protamine sulfate
Atropine sulfate

rationale.correct: Support the airway first; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and naloxone reverses opioids.

perOption.a: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines such as midazolam.
perOption.b: Naloxone reverses opioids, which were not given.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose the reversal agent for benzodiazepine sedation.

questions.stem: A client 6 hours after a thoracotomy is receiving hydromorphone through an epidural catheter and has had a dose of IV morphine for breakthrough pain. Which assessment is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Respiratory rate and sedation level
Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Skin turgor over the forearm
Appetite and fluid intake

rationale.correct: Epidural analgesia: monitor breathing, sedation, blood pressure, motor block and the catheter site.

perOption.a: Epidural opioids can cause delayed respiratory depression, and other opioids add to the risk.
perOption.b: This is not the priority.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old client who takes two blood pressure medicines is about to walk for the first time after a colectomy. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Have the client sit on the edge of the bed for a few minutes
Help the client stand up quickly, before any dizziness can start
Give the prescribed sedative so the client stays calm
Keep the client lying flat for 1 hour before standing

rationale.correct: First walk: raise the head of the bed, dangle the legs, stand with help and watch for dizziness.

perOption.a: Dangling the legs lets the blood pressure adjust and reduces fainting.
perOption.b: Standing quickly causes orthostatic hypotension.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Help a client walk safely for the first time after surgery.

questions.stem: A client has a Jackson-Pratt drain after a mastectomy. The bulb is half full and fully rounded. How should the nurse manage the drain?

options.text: Empty and measure it, then squeeze the bulb and close it
Leave the bulb fully rounded so that the fluid drains freely
Empty it once a day, at the end of the night shift
Flush the drain tubing with saline to keep it open

rationale.correct: Jackson-Pratt drain: empty, measure, compress, close and record.

perOption.a: Compressing the bulb before closing creates the suction that draws fluid out.
perOption.b: A rounded bulb provides no suction.
perOption.c: It is emptied when about half full.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client is newly confused and pulling at the IV on the first night after a hip repair. The client was fully oriented before surgery. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check the oxygen saturation and vital signs
Apply soft wrist restraints to protect the IV
Give the PRN lorazepam so the client can sleep
Call the family to come and sit with the client

rationale.correct: Postoperative delirium: look for causes (hypoxia, infection, pain, drugs, urinary retention) and reorient the client.

perOption.a: Hypoxia is a common, treatable cause of delirium.
perOption.b: Restraints worsen delirium and are a last resort.
perOption.d: Family can help, but a cause must be looked for first.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client 2 days after abdominal surgery is wearing sequential compression devices and reports new pain and swelling in the right calf. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remove the device from the right leg and notify the provider
Increase the device pressure to improve the blood flow in the leg
Massage the calf gently to ease the pain and swelling
Encourage the client to walk more often around the unit

rationale.correct: Suspected DVT: do not massage or compress the leg; notify the provider for evaluation.

perOption.a: Compression could dislodge a clot, and a DVT needs evaluation.
perOption.b: This could dislodge a clot.
perOption.d: Activity is limited until DVT is ruled out.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to suspected DVT with compression devices.

questions.stem: A client is going home 3 hours after an outpatient knee arthroscopy under general anesthesia. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "My wife will drive me home and stay with me tonight."
"I'll drive myself to my evening shift if I feel fine."
"I'll keep my leg up and use ice as I was shown."
"I won't have any alcohol for the rest of the day today."

rationale.correct: After anesthesia: no driving, alcohol or important decisions for 24 hours, and a responsible adult present.

perOption.a: A responsible adult should drive and stay overnight.
perOption.b: Clients do not drive or make important decisions for 24 hours after anesthesia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing findings for a client 8 hours after an open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. Select the 3 findings that require immediate follow-up.

options.text: SpO2 of 89% on 2 L/min
Urine output of 20 mL/hr for 2 hours
Blood pressure of 86/50 mm Hg
Pain rated 4 out of 10
Temperature of 37.6 °C (99.7 °F)
Serosanguineous spots on the dressing

rationale.correct: Report hypoxemia, low urine output and hypotension promptly after surgery.

perOption.a: Hypoxemia needs action now.
perOption.b: Low output suggests hypovolemia or kidney injury.
perOption.e: A mild temperature is common after surgery.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client who takes furosemide is scheduled for a hip replacement at 0800. The 0600 laboratory results show a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the surgeon and anesthesia provider before surgery
Continue the preparation, since the level is slightly low
Give the client a banana and a glass of orange juice
Ask for the test to be repeated after the surgery

rationale.correct: Report abnormal preoperative labs (potassium, glucose, hemoglobin, coagulation) before surgery.

perOption.a: Hypokalemia raises the risk of dysrhythmias under anesthesia.
perOption.b: This ignores a significant abnormality.
perOption.c: This does not correct it before surgery, and the client is NPO.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On the first morning after a laparoscopic appendectomy, the nurse finds a small amount of pink, watery drainage on one port-site dressing. Vital signs are normal. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Document it as expected and keep monitoring
Notify the surgeon of a possible wound infection
Remove the dressing and leave the site open to air
Apply a heat pack over the dressing to dry it

rationale.correct: Know what is expected after surgery and what needs reporting: large amounts, bright red or purulent drainage.

perOption.a: A small amount of serosanguineous drainage is expected early.
perOption.b: This is expected, not a sign of infection.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
